reading.body:
Every dollar of income falls in one of three buckets, and losses generally cannot jump buckets. **Earned/active** income is wages and self-employment. **Portfolio** income is interest, dividends, and capital gains. **Passive** income is from DPPs and rental real estate.

The rule that follows: a **passive loss offsets only passive income** — never wages, never interest or dividends. Keeping the buckets straight is what makes DPP-suitability and net-loss questions solvable, because the exam deliberately mixes salary, dividends, and partnership income in one stem to see whether you'll wrongly net them together.

reading.h: Capital gains, holding period, and rate buckets
reading.body:
**Long-term = held MORE than one year.** Buy January 15, 2025; a sale on January 15, 2026 is still short-term, but January 16, 2026 is long-term. The clock uses the **trade date**, not settlement, for both the buy and the sell.

**Short-term gains** are taxed as ordinary income. **Long-term capital gains and qualified dividends** get the preferential **0% / 15% / 20%** rates. High earners also owe the **3.8% net investment income tax (NIIT)** on the lesser of net investment income or income above a threshold. **Qualified dividends** must be paid by a U.S. or qualified foreign corporation on stock held **more than 60 days** in the 121-day window around the ex-date; REIT dividends, money-market dividends, and short-term gain distributions are **non-qualified** (ordinary).

**Cost basis** = purchase price + commissions, adjusted up for reinvested distributions and disallowed wash-sale losses, and down for return of capital. After a stock split or stock dividend the total cost is unchanged — only the **per-share** basis changes (100 shares at $125 with a 25% stock dividend → 125 shares at $100).

When you sell part of a position, the method decides the gain. **FIFO** is the **IRS default** — oldest shares first, usually the largest gain in a rising market. **Specific identification** lets you name the lots (lowest tax) but you must instruct the broker at the time of sale. **Average cost** is allowed **only for mutual funds and DRIPs**. Worked lots of 100 @ $10, $20, $30, selling 100 at $25: FIFO shows a $1,500 gain; specific-ID of the $30 lot shows a $500 loss; average ($20) shows a $500 gain.

Netting runs in two steps. **Step 1:** net short-term gains against short-term losses, and separately net long-term gains against long-term losses. **Step 2:** if one side is a gain and the other a loss, net the two together.

Worked example: ST gain $5,000, ST loss $8,000, LT gain $10,000, LT loss $4,000. Step 1 → net ST **loss $3,000** and net LT **gain $6,000**. Step 2 → net them → a **net long-term gain of $3,000**, taxed at LTCG rates.

If the final result is a **net capital loss**, you may deduct up to **$3,000 per year** ($1,500 if married filing separately) against ordinary income; the **excess carries forward indefinitely**, keeping its short- or long-term character. A $10,000 net loss means $3,000 this year and $7,000 carried forward.

The **wash-sale rule (IRC §1091)** disallows a **loss** if you buy **substantially identical** securities within **30 days before or after** the sale — a **61-day window**. "Substantially identical" includes the same stock and **calls, rights, warrants, or convertibles on that stock**, plus the same fund; it does **not** include a different company in the same industry.

The disallowed loss is **added to the basis** of the replacement shares, and the old **holding period tacks on** — so nothing is lost forever, just deferred. Two exceptions to remember: buying the replacement inside an **IRA** disallows the loss **permanently** (no basis add-back), and the rule applies to **losses only** — gains are always recognized. For **bonds**, two of three terms (issuer, coupon, maturity) must differ to avoid being substantially identical.

reading.h: Gifted securities and the dual-basis rule
reading.body:
A **gift** normally carries over the **donor's basis and holding period** to the donee. The wrinkle is the **dual-basis rule** when the **FMV at the gift date is below the donor's basis**: for a later **gain**, use the donor's (higher) basis; for a later **loss**, use the (lower) gift-date FMV; a sale **between** the two produces **no gain or loss**.

Worked example: donor's basis $50, FMV at the gift $30. Daughter sells at $25 → loss measured from $30 = **$500 loss** (using the FMV, so the donor's holding period does not tack on and the loss is short-term). Sell at $60 → gain from $50. Sell at $40 → **no gain or loss**. The donor, not the recipient, owes any gift tax, and receiving the gift is not income to the recipient.

reading.h: Inherited securities and return of capital
reading.body:
**Inherited** securities get a **stepped-up (or down) basis equal to FMV on the date of death** (or the alternate valuation date six months later if the executor elects it), and the holding period is **always long-term** regardless of how long anyone held them.

Example: the decedent bought at $20 and died when the stock was $100; the heir sells one month later at $110 → a **$1,000 long-term gain** (110 − 100 stepped-up basis). One trap: assets inside an **IRA, annuity, or 401(k) get no step-up** (income in respect of a decedent).

Finally, a **return of capital** (a distribution exceeding earnings, common in REITs and MLPs) is **not taxed when received**; it **reduces basis**, and once basis reaches zero, further return of capital is taxed as **capital gain**.

flashcards.back: Earned/active (wages), portfolio (interest, dividends, gains), passive (DPPs, rental). Passive losses offset only passive income.
MORE than one year, measured from the TRADE date (not settlement). Exactly one year = still short-term.
0% / 15% / 20%, plus a 3.8% NIIT for high earners. Short-term gains are ordinary income.

flashcards.front: FIFO vs. specific ID vs. average cost
flashcards.back: FIFO = IRS default (oldest first). Specific ID = name the lots at sale (lowest tax). Average cost = mutual funds/DRIPs only.
Up to $3,000/yr ($1,500 MFS) against ordinary income; excess carries forward indefinitely, keeping its ST/LT character.
Loss disallowed if substantially identical securities bought within 30 days before OR after the sale (61-day window).

flashcards.front: Wash sale — what happens to the disallowed loss?
flashcards.back: Added to the basis of the replacement shares; old holding period tacks on. In an IRA it is disallowed PERMANENTLY (no add-back).
Same stock, plus calls/rights/warrants/convertibles on it, and the same fund. NOT a competitor's stock in the same industry.
FMV at gift below donor basis: use donor basis for a GAIN, gift-date FMV for a LOSS; a sale between = no gain or loss.
Stepped up to FMV at date of death (or alternate date 6 months later); ALWAYS long-term. No step-up inside an IRA/annuity/401(k).
Stock held more than 60 days in the 121-day window around the ex-date (91/181 for certain preferred).
Not taxed when received; reduces basis. Once basis hits zero, further ROC is taxed as capital gain.

quiz.stem: A father gives his daughter 100 shares he purchased for $50 per share. On the gift date the stock trades at $30. Eight months later she sells all 100 shares at $25. For tax purposes she reports:
quiz.explanation: When FMV at the gift date ($30) is below the donor's basis ($50), a later loss is measured from the gift-date FMV: ($30 − $25) × 100 = $500 loss. The donor's $50 basis would apply only to a gain, and a sale between $30 and $50 would produce neither gain nor loss.

quiz.stem: A man bought 100 shares of ABC at $20 and died two months later when ABC was $100. His daughter inherited the shares and sold them one month after his death at $110. She reports:
quiz.explanation: Inherited securities take a stepped-up basis equal to FMV at the date of death ($100) and are always treated as long-term regardless of how long anyone held them: ($110 − $100) × 100 = $1,000 long-term gain.

quiz.stem: A customer sells 500 shares of XYZ common at a loss on June 1. All of the following purchases on June 15 would disallow the loss under the wash-sale rule EXCEPT:
options: Common stock of XYZ's largest competitor in the same industry
XYZ common stock purchased in the customer's IRA
quiz.explanation: Within the 30-day window, calls, convertibles, and rights on the same stock are substantially identical, and a repurchase inside an IRA disallows the loss permanently. A different company's stock, even in the same industry, is NOT substantially identical, so it does not trigger the rule.

quiz.stem: For the year a customer has a short-term gain of $5,000, a short-term loss of $8,000, a long-term gain of $10,000, and a long-term loss of $4,000. The net result is:
quiz.explanation: Step 1: net ST → $5,000 − $8,000 = $3,000 ST loss; net LT → $10,000 − $4,000 = $6,000 LT gain. Step 2: net the two → $6,000 − $3,000 = a net long-term gain of $3,000, taxed at LTCG rates.

quiz.stem: A customer buys stock on January 15, 2025. To receive long-term capital gain treatment on a later sale, the EARLIEST the customer may sell is:
quiz.explanation: Long-term treatment requires holding MORE than one year, measured from the trade date. A sale exactly one year later (January 15, 2026) is still short-term; January 16, 2026 is the first long-term day. Settlement date is not used for the holding period.

quiz.stem: A customer realizes a $1,000 loss selling XYZ on March 1 and buys the same XYZ shares on March 20. The disallowed wash-sale loss is:
options: Deductible in full because the repurchase was more than 15 days later
Added to the basis of the newly purchased shares, with the old holding period tacking on
quiz.explanation: The disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement shares and the prior holding period tacks on, so the benefit is deferred, not lost — unless the repurchase was made in an IRA, which forfeits it permanently. The 61-day window covers 30 days before and after, so March 20 is inside it.

quiz.stem: A REIT distribution classified as a return of capital is:
options: Taxed as ordinary income in the year received
Not taxed when received; it reduces the shareholder's cost basis
Taxed as a long-term capital gain regardless of holding period
quiz.explanation: A return of capital is not taxed when received; it reduces cost basis. Once basis reaches zero, any further return of capital is taxed as a capital gain — so it defers tax rather than eliminating it.

quiz.stem: When a customer sells part of a position and does not identify specific shares at the time of sale, the IRS default method for determining cost basis is:
quiz.explanation: FIFO is the IRS default absent specific identification — the oldest shares are treated as sold first, usually producing the largest gain in a rising market. Average cost is available only for mutual funds and DRIPs, and LIFO is not an IRS method for securities.
